systems.title: The Linux kernel
systems.claim: The Linux kernel is one program, developed in the open, that thousands of people change every nine weeks or so. Its 7.3 release in October 2026 took in 18,765 non-merge commits from 3,021 developers.

facts.text: Linux 7.3 was released on October 18, 2026. The cycle had 18,765 non-merge commits from 3,021 developers, a record, and 807 of them were first-time contributors.
Those commits added nearly 920,000 lines and removed just over 270,000, a net growth of about 650,000 lines in one cycle.
The kernel's own documentation says it is written mostly in C, with some architecture-dependent parts in assembly.
The kernel documentation has a section for Rust code within the kernel, with a quick start guide, coding guidelines and a list of supported architectures.
On November 24, 2026 kernel.org listed 7.3.6 as the latest stable release and 7.4-rc4 as mainline.

systems.caveat: Solid for the per-release numbers: LWN computes them from the public git history each cycle. No total line count is given here because none of the sources fetched states one; published totals depend on what is counted (comments, generated files, documentation).

systems.title: What runs on Linux
systems.claim: Every one of the 500 fastest ranked supercomputers runs Linux, and the Android kernel is built from the upstream Linux kernel.

facts.text: In the November 2026 TOP500 list, the operating system family statistics show Linux on 500 of 500 systems.
Android's documentation states that the Android kernel is based on an upstream Linux Long Term Supported (LTS) kernel, combined with Android-specific patches to form Android Common Kernels.

systems.caveat: Solid. TOP500 only covers machines whose owners submit benchmark results, so it is a statement about the ranked list, not about every large computer. The TOP500 figure comes from the site's List Statistics form (select November 2026 and Operating system Family). No Android device count is given because no primary figure was fetched.

systems.title: The internet's core protocols
systems.claim: The internet is defined by public documents called RFCs, and code everywhere implements them. IP, TCP, DNS, BGP and TLS each have a specification anyone can read, and those specifications are still being revised.

facts.text: RFC 791, Internet Protocol, by Jon Postel, is dated September 1981 and is an Internet Standard (STD 5).
RFC 9293, Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), was published in August 2022 as Internet Standard STD 7. It replaced the original TCP specification, RFC 793, and six later documents.
RFC 1035, Domain Names: Implementation and Specification, by Paul Mockapetris, is dated November 1987 and is part of Internet Standard STD 13.
RFC 4271, A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4), dated January 2006, specifies the routing protocol used between autonomous systems.
RFC 9846, The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3, was published in July 2026 and obsoletes RFC 8446, the August 2018 specification of TLS 1.3.
The IETF, which produces these documents, has no formal membership. Participants are volunteers, and working groups decide by rough consensus instead of voting.

systems.caveat: Solid: these are the specifications themselves. An RFC describes behavior, not any one implementation, so no programming language is listed. Each of these protocols also has later RFCs that extend it.

systems.title: The web
systems.claim: The web rests on two public specifications, HTTP and HTML, and on the browsers that implement them. HTML has no final version: its specification is a Living Standard that is edited continuously.

facts.text: RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, was published in June 2022 as Internet Standard STD 97. It defines the parts of HTTP shared by all versions, including the http and https URI schemes.
The HTML specification is published by WHATWG as a Living Standard. On the day it was checked, its header read: Last Updated 24 November 2026.
The same document records that in 2019 WHATWG and W3C agreed to work together on a single version of HTML, and that HTML's first years (1990 to 1995) were hosted at CERN and then at the IETF.
Chromium describes itself as an open-source browser project, and the Chromium projects as the open-source projects behind the Google Chrome browser.

systems.caveat: Solid for the specifications. No browser engine size and no browser market share is given: no primary source for either was fetched.

systems.title: Payments and bank messaging
systems.claim: Card payments and bank-to-bank messages are software services running at very large scale. Visa reports 329 billion transactions in a year, and Swift reports more than 53 million FIN messages a day.

facts.text: Visa's fact sheet reports 329 billion total transactions and 17 trillion US dollars in total volume for the 12 months ended September 30, 2025, across more than 200 countries and territories and about 14,500 financial institutions.
Swift describes itself as a cooperative of more than 12,500 institutions, founded in 1973, sending on average more than 53 million FIN messages every day, with 99.99% FIN availability in 2024.

systems.caveat: The numbers are the companies' own published figures, not independent measurements. Visa's totals include cash transactions as well as payments. Neither source says what languages the systems are written in, so none is listed. Swift carries messages about payments; it does not itself hold or move money.

systems.title: Mainframes, COBOL and assembly in government
systems.claim: Some of the systems that assess taxes and pay benefits in the United States are decades old and written in COBOL or assembly language. This is documented by the Government Accountability Office, system by system.

facts.text: GAO reported in 2016 that the Treasury's Individual Master File, the authoritative data source for individual taxpayers, was about 56 years old, written in assembly language and running on an IBM mainframe.

The same report lists a Department of Veterans Affairs time and attendance system written in COBOL on IBM mainframes, reported as 53 years old, and a Defense system coordinating nuclear forces that still used 8-inch floppy disks.
In 2019 GAO examined the ten most critical federal legacy systems and found them to be 8 to 51 years old. It noted that the Department of Education's selected system runs on COBOL.
COBOL is still a supported product: IBM sells Enterprise COBOL for z/OS, with version 6.5 documentation current in November 2026, and says it normally ships a fix pack every two months.

systems.caveat: Solid, but narrow and dated: these are United States federal systems as reported by the agencies in 2016 and 2019, and some have since been modernized or scheduled for replacement. No global figure for lines of COBOL or for the share of banking that runs on mainframes is given, because no primary source for one was found. gao.gov refuses some automated requests; the pages open in a browser.

systems.title: Airborne software
systems.claim: Software on certified aircraft is developed under a specific assurance standard, DO-178C, which the FAA recognizes as an acceptable way to show compliance with airworthiness regulations.

facts.text: FAA Advisory Circular 20-115D, issued July 21, 2017, recognizes RTCA DO-178C, Software Considerations in Airborne Systems and Equipment Certification (dated December 13, 2011), and its European twin EUROCAE ED-12C.

The circular describes this as an acceptable means, but not the only means, of showing compliance for the software aspects of airborne systems and equipment. It also recognizes supplements for tool qualification (DO-330), model-based development (DO-331), object-oriented technology (DO-332) and formal methods (DO-333).

systems.caveat: Solid on the regulatory fact. DO-178C itself is sold by RTCA and was not read. No language list and no line count for any aircraft is given, because no primary source was fetched.

systems.title: Spaceflight software
systems.claim: The code that flew Apollo 11 is public and readable today, and current missions run on software that NASA publishes as open source or describes in detail.

facts.text: The Apollo 11 guidance computer source code for the Command Module (Comanche055) and the Lunar Module (Luminary099) is public domain and online, digitized by Virtual AGC and the MIT Museum. The listings are dated April 1 and July 14, 1969 and are assembled with the yaYUL assembler.
NASA's Ingenuity Mars helicopter, which first flew on April 19, 2021, used F Prime, a flight software framework created at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in 2013 and released as open source in 2017.
F Prime is published by NASA under the Apache 2.0 license as a flight software and embedded systems framework; its repository is tagged cpp.

The onboard scripts that run observations on the James Webb Space Telescope are written in JavaScript, according to the Space Telescope Science Institute. They let the telescope skip a visit or stop commanding an instrument on its own when something goes wrong.

systems.caveat: Solid. The Apollo repository is a transcription from scanned listings, so it can contain transcription errors. The NASA article says Ingenuity also used an open-source operating system but does not name it, so it is not named here.

systems.title: Medical device software
systems.claim: Software that is part of a medical device is regulated: in the United States the FDA tells manufacturers what software documentation a premarket submission should contain, and it recognizes IEC 62304 as the standard for the software life cycle.

facts.text: FDA's guidance Content of Premarket Submissions for Device Software Functions was issued in June 2023 and replaced the agency's 2005 guidance on software in medical devices.

FDA lists IEC 62304 Edition 1.1 (2015), Medical device software: Software life cycle processes, as a recognized consensus standard, recognition number 13-79, entered January 14, 2019, recognized as a complete standard.

systems.caveat: Solid on the regulatory facts, for the United States only. IEC 62304 itself is a paid standard and was not read. No count of software-driven devices or recalls is given.

systems.title: Industrial control
systems.claim: The programmable controllers that run factories and plants have their own standardized family of programming languages, defined in IEC 61131-3.

facts.text: IEC 61131-3:2013 specifies the syntax and semantics of a unified suite of programming languages for programmable controllers: two textual languages, Instruction List and Structured Text, and two graphical languages, Ladder Diagram and Function Block Diagram.
The 2013 text is the third edition and replaced the second edition of 2003. The IEC catalog marks it as revised, meaning a newer edition has since been published.

systems.caveat: Solid for what the 2013 edition defines, taken from the IEC's own abstract. The newer edition was not checked, so its language list is not stated. None of these languages is in this site's language list. No claim is made about how much of the power grid or industry they control.

systems.title: Cars
systems.claim: Car makers and suppliers share a standardized software architecture, AUTOSAR, and a functional safety standard, ISO 26262, for the electronics in series production road vehicles.

facts.text: AUTOSAR's initial development agreement was signed by its core partners in July 2003. Releases R25-11 of the Classic, Adaptive and Foundation standards were published in December 2025.

AUTOSAR says most of the signals and control values in a vehicle are supplied and processed by the Classic Platform, while the Adaptive Platform is a runtime environment for applications on microprocessor systems that runs on a POSIX-based operating system.

ISO 26262-1:2018 (Part 1 of the series Road vehicles: Functional safety, second edition) says the series applies to safety-related electrical and electronic systems installed in series production road vehicles, excluding mopeds. ISO lists a draft revision of this part as expected to replace it.

systems.caveat: Solid on what the standards are. The often repeated claim that a car contains 100 million lines of code has no primary source that could be found and is left out. iso.org refuses automated requests (HTTP 403); the page was read in a browser.

systems.title: Scientific computing
systems.claim: Weather forecasts, particle physics and numerical work in general depend on long-lived shared code, much of it in Fortran and C++.

facts.text: ECMWF says much of its Integrated Forecasting System is written in Fortran, alongside shell scripts and Python.
The most recent model cycle ECMWF lists, 50r1, went into operation on May 12, 2026.

An ECMWF article on modernizing the system calls it mission-critical software to which hundreds of people have contributed over decades, and warns that it will become harder to find software engineers willing to work on older frameworks and languages such as Fortran.
ROOT, the data analysis framework from CERN, saves data and any C++ object in compressed binary files, ships a C++ interpreter (Cling) and has bindings for Python and R.

LAPACK, the standard linear algebra library, is written in Fortran 90 and is provided by the University of Tennessee, UC Berkeley, the University of Colorado Denver and NAG Ltd. The current version is 3.12.1.

systems.caveat: Solid, from the projects themselves. These are examples, not a survey: no share of scientific code by language is claimed. LIGO and Event Horizon Telescope software were not researched in this pass.

systems.title: OpenSSL and encrypted connections
systems.claim: OpenSSL is an open source toolkit that implements TLS, the protocol used to encrypt connections on the internet. One missing bounds check in it, found in 2014, exposed the memory of servers around the world.

facts.text: The project describes OpenSSL as a robust, commercial-grade, full-featured open source toolkit for the TLS (formerly SSL), DTLS and QUIC protocols.

The Heartbleed site, written by the team that co-discovered the bug, noted that Apache and nginx, the two best known web servers using OpenSSL, had a combined share of over 66% of active sites in Netcraft's April 2014 survey.

systems.caveat: The description is solid. The 66% figure is from 2014, is a share of web server software and not of OpenSSL itself, and is only an indication of reach. No current deployment share is given. The language (C) is well known but was not shown on the pages fetched.

systems.title: SQLite
systems.claim: SQLite is a small database library built into phones, browsers and operating systems. Its developers estimate that it is probably one of the five most deployed software modules of any kind.

facts.text: The SQLite project says SQLite is likely used more than all other database engines combined, and lists every Android device, every iPhone, every Mac, every Windows 10 and 11 installation and every Firefox, Chrome and Safari browser among its users.
From more than 4 billion smartphones in active use, each holding hundreds of SQLite database files, the project estimates over one trillion SQLite databases in active use.
The project's best guess is that SQLite is the second most widely deployed software library, after zlib.

systems.caveat: These are the project's own estimates, and the page says so: precise numbers are difficult to obtain and exact rankings are impossible. The trillion figure is an extrapolation from a smartphone count, not a measurement. The implementation language (C) is well known but was not shown on the page fetched.

systems.title: Open source as shared infrastructure
systems.claim: Programs are assembled from open source packages that anyone can publish and anyone can use. The public registries that hold them now contain millions of packages.

facts.text: GitHub's Octoverse 2025 report, covering September 1, 2024 through August 31, 2025, counts more than 180 million developers, 630 million total repositories (121 million of them new in the period) and 395 million public and open source repositories.
The npm registry's public replication endpoint reported 4,648,384 documents (roughly, packages) on November 24, 2026.
The Python Package Index showed 950,745 projects, 10,304,042 releases and 23,201,577 files on November 24, 2026.
crates.io, the Rust package registry, reported 386,729 crates and about 578.6 billion downloads in total on November 24, 2026.

systems.caveat: Registry counts are live numbers read on the date shown and change daily. They count published names, including abandoned, trivial and spam packages, so they measure size, not quality or use. The npm figure is a document count from the registry database and may differ slightly from the number of installable packages. GitHub's figures are the company's own.

systems.title: Proved software in production
systems.claim: A few programs in real use come with machine-checked mathematical proofs that the code does what its specification says. The seL4 microkernel and the CompCert C compiler are the best known.

facts.text: seL4 has machine-checked proofs, written in Isabelle/HOL, for Arm, RISC-V and Intel architectures: functional correctness of the C code against its specification and, in supporting configurations, correctness of the binary and the security properties integrity, availability and confidentiality.

The seL4 Foundation lists products built on seL4, including the SkyOS-M operating system in NIO's mass-produced ONVO L60 electric car and a voice communication system used by air traffic and maritime controllers.

CompCert is a compiler for almost all of ISO C 2011 with a machine-checked proof that the generated code behaves as the source program does. Its proofs are developed in Rocq, it targets ARM, PowerPC, RISC-V and x86, and it is aimed at critical embedded software.

CompCert was qualified for the MFC_NG flight computer of ATR 42/72 aircraft, which the project describes as the first time certification credits under DO-178C, DO-333 and DO-330 could be claimed from the use of a compiler.

systems.caveat: Solid, from the projects' own pages. The proofs hold under stated assumptions and, for seL4, not every property is proved on every platform and configuration. Deployment lists are self-reported by the projects.

systems.title: Models as software in the world
systems.claim: Trained neural networks are now distributed and versioned like software packages. One public hub alone lists more than three million of them.

facts.text: The Hugging Face Hub's model listing reported 3,269,936 models on November 24, 2026.
GitHub's Octoverse 2025 report says TypeScript became the most used language on GitHub in the period measured, and its title credits AI for that.

systems.caveat: The count is a live number and includes duplicates, fine-tunes, quantized copies and abandoned uploads, so it measures how many artifacts are published, not how many distinct or useful models exist. No figure for how much of the world's software now calls or is written by a model is given: no solid source was found. Python is listed as the usual language of the tooling, not from a fetched source.

failures.title: Therac-25 radiation overdoses
failures.what: Between June 1985 and January 1987, a computer-controlled radiation therapy machine gave six known patients massive overdoses, causing deaths and serious injuries. One fault was a race condition: if the operator edited the treatment settings and returned to the command line within about 8 seconds, the software never noticed the edit. Earlier machines had hardware interlocks that masked the same kind of error; the Therac-25 relied on software for those safety functions.
failures.lesson: Software that replaces a physical safety mechanism has to be engineered and checked as a safety mechanism, and reused code is not safe just because it ran before.

failures.title: Ariane 5 flight 501
failures.what: On June 4, 1996, about 37 seconds after main engine ignition, software in both inertial reference systems tried to convert a 64-bit floating point number into a 16-bit signed integer. The value was too large, the unprotected Ada conversion raised an error, and both units shut down. The rocket lost its guidance data, veered off course, broke up and destroyed itself on its maiden flight. The code that failed was an alignment routine kept from Ariane 4 that had no purpose after lift-off.
failures.lesson: Code that was correct for one machine carries its assumptions with it, and they have to be checked again when it is reused.

failures.title: Mars Climate Orbiter
failures.what: A ground software file called Small Forces reported thruster impulse in English units (pound-force seconds) where the specification required metric units (newton seconds), a factor of 4.45. Over the nine-month cruise the small errors accumulated in the trajectory estimate, and on September 23, 1999 the spacecraft reached Mars about 170 kilometers lower than planned. It was destroyed in the atmosphere or passed back into space, and was lost.
failures.lesson: The interface between two programs is part of the program, including the units of every number that crosses it.

failures.title: The Year 2000 remediation
failures.what: Many programs stored years as two digits, so the year 2000 could be read as 1900. Instead of a disaster this became a very large repair job: the United States Senate's special committee reported that the country spent an estimated 100 billion dollars on the problem, 8.5 billion of it in the federal government. The committee's final report, dated February 29, 2000, is titled Y2K Aftermath: Crisis Averted.
failures.lesson: A shortcut in a data format can outlive its authors by decades, and maintenance done in time looks afterward as if nothing happened.

failures.title: Knight Capital
failures.what: On August 1, 2012, a trading firm's automated order router ran a defective function that had been left in its code since 2005, after new code was deployed incorrectly in late July. In the first 45 minutes of trading it sent more than 4 million orders while trying to fill 212 customer orders and traded more than 397 million shares. The firm lost more than 460 million dollars and later paid a 12 million dollar penalty to the SEC.
failures.lesson: Dead code that stays in a system is still code, and a deployment is part of the program's correctness.

failures.title: Heartbleed
failures.what: A missing bounds check in OpenSSL's implementation of the TLS heartbeat extension let anyone on the internet read up to 64 kilobytes of a server's or client's memory per request, which could include secret keys and passwords. The bug shipped in OpenSSL 1.0.1 in March 2012 and was fixed in version 1.0.1g on April 7, 2014. It was found by Neel Mehta of Google Security and, independently, by a team at Codenomicon.
failures.lesson: A library that almost everyone depends on can go years with a simple flaw in it when few people are looking.

failures.title: The left-pad incident
failures.what: On March 22, 2016, after a dispute over a package name, a developer removed 273 of his packages from the npm registry, among them a tiny one called left-pad. Many thousands of projects depended on it directly or through other packages, and npm saw hundreds of failed installs per minute. Within ten minutes another developer published a functionally identical replacement.
failures.lesson: A program depends on everything its dependencies depend on, and on those things staying published.

failures.title: Log4Shell
failures.what: Log4j, a Java logging library embedded in thousands of other software packages, would follow lookups placed inside logged text, so an attacker who could get a string logged could make the server load and run code from a remote address. The feature had been added in 2013; the flaw was reported to Apache on November 24, 2021, became public on December 9, and was rated 10.0, the maximum severity. The United States Cyber Safety Review Board called it an endemic vulnerability that will remain in systems for perhaps a decade or longer.
failures.lesson: A convenience feature in a widely embedded library can become an entry point into every system that includes it, and removing it everywhere takes years.

failures.title: The xz utils backdoor
failures.what: On March 29, 2024, engineer Andres Freund reported that the release archives of the compression tool xz, versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1, contained a deliberately hidden backdoor, part of it present only in the distributed archives and not in the source repository. He found it while investigating why ssh logins on a Debian test system were using a lot of processor time. The versions had not yet been widely adopted, mostly reaching pre-release distributions; the issue is tracked as CVE-2024-3094.
failures.lesson: A widely used component maintained by very few people is a target, and what gets shipped has to be checkable against the source.

failures.title: The CrowdStrike outage
failures.what: On July 19, 2024, a security vendor delivered a content update whose new template expected 21 input fields, while the sensor code on each Windows machine supplied only 20. With no runtime bounds check, reading the 21st value went past the end of the array in the sensor's Content Interpreter and crashed the system. Microsoft estimated that 8.5 million Windows devices were affected, less than one percent of all Windows machines.
failures.lesson: Data that steers privileged code is effectively code, and it needs the same validation, testing and staged rollout.

living.title: Versions
living.text: Software is released again and again, and each release gets a number that tells users what changed. Semantic Versioning is a published convention for those numbers: a version is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and which part increases says whether upgrading can break you.

facts.text: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0: increment MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for functionality added in a backward compatible manner, PATCH for backward compatible bug fixes. The specification was originally written by Tom Preston-Werner.
The Linux kernel showed two live lines on the same day: stable release 7.3.6 and mainline candidate 7.4-rc4.

living.title: Dependencies and supply chains
living.text: Almost no program is written from nothing. It pulls in packages, which pull in other packages, and the result is a tree of code written by people the author has never met. That tree is the program's supply chain, and it can break or be attacked at any link.

facts.text: A 2019 study of the npm ecosystem (data through April 2018) found that installing an average npm package means implicitly trusting 79 third-party packages and 39 maintainers.
In March 2016 the removal of one small package, left-pad, caused hundreds of failed installs per minute across the npm registry.
In March 2024 a backdoor was found in release archives of xz, a compression tool that many systems include indirectly.

living.title: Maintenance
living.text: A program in use keeps needing work: fixing faults, adapting to new hardware, laws and neighboring systems, and keeping it running. There is no single agreed percentage for this, so none is given here, but one well documented budget shows the shape of it.

facts.text: The United States federal government spent about 75 percent of its total information technology budget for fiscal year 2015 on operations and maintenance, and 5,233 of its roughly 7,000 IT investments spent all of their funds that way.
The Cyber Safety Review Board expects vulnerable copies of Log4j to remain in systems for many years, perhaps a decade or longer, after the fix was published.

living.caveat: The 75 percent figure covers operating and maintaining IT systems (hardware, services and software together) in one government in one year. It is not a measurement of the share of software cost that is maintenance.

living.title: Version control
living.text: Code is kept as a history of changes, not as a pile of files. Each change records who made it, when and why, and any earlier state can be recovered. The tool almost everyone uses for this, Git, was written for the Linux kernel.

facts.text: The Linux kernel project used the proprietary system BitKeeper from 2002. When its free-of-charge status was revoked in 2005, the kernel community, and in particular Linus Torvalds, built Git, aiming for speed, a simple design, strong support for thousands of parallel branches, full distribution and efficient handling of projects as large as the kernel.
GitHub, a hosting service built on Git, reported 630 million repositories in its 2025 Octoverse report.

living.title: Code review
living.text: In most serious projects a change is read by someone other than its author before it is accepted. Review catches faults, spreads knowledge of the code and leaves a record of who vouched for what.

facts.text: In the Linux kernel, a Reviewed-by tag is a statement of opinion that the patch is an appropriate modification of the kernel, given by someone who has carried out a technical review of it. A Signed-off-by tag certifies that the submitter has the right to contribute the code.

A 2018 study of code review at Google analyzed 9 million reviewed changes and found that the median developer authors about 3 changes a week and that the median time for the entire review process is under 4 hours.

living.title: Long-lived code
living.text: Working code tends to stay. Systems written half a century ago were still in daily service when last reported, and numerical libraries from earlier decades are still being released. Old code stays because it is in use.

facts.text: In 2016 the United States Treasury's Individual Master File, which assesses taxes and generates refunds for individual taxpayers, was reported as about 56 years old and written in assembly language.
The Apollo 11 guidance computer listings from 1969 are public, and the repository points to the Virtual AGC project for anyone who wants to compile them.
LAPACK, written in Fortran 90, is still provided by four institutions and stood at version 3.12.1 in November 2026.

living.caveat: The 56-year age is the agency's own report from 2016. No claim is made about which code is the oldest still in use anywhere; no source establishes that.

living.title: Bit rot and changing foundations
living.text: A program that is never touched still stops working, because everything under it keeps changing: languages, libraries, operating systems and protocols. Keeping software alive means moving with them.

facts.text: Python 2 was retired on January 1, 2020. Work on Python 3.0 began in 2006, and the retirement date, first announced in 2008 as 2015, was extended to 2020 in 2014 because so much code had not moved.
Even core internet standards are replaced: the 2018 specification of TLS 1.3, RFC 8446, was obsoleted by RFC 9846 in July 2026, and in 2022 RFC 9293 replaced the original TCP specification.
The HTML specification is a Living Standard with no final version; its header showed an update on the day it was checked.

living.title: Reproducible builds
living.text: People read source code, but machines run binaries, and the step between them is usually taken on trust. A build is reproducible when others can rebuild the same source and check that they get the same result, which makes tampering in between detectable.

facts.text: The Reproducible Builds project defines reproducible builds as a set of software development practices that create an independently verifiable path from source to binary code.
The xz backdoor of 2024 was partly present only in the distributed release archives and not in the source repository, which is the gap this practice is meant to close.

living.title: Preserving source code
living.text: Source code is a record of how things work, and it disappears when hosting sites close or projects are deleted. Software Heritage collects and preserves software in source code form.

facts.text: Software Heritage states its mission as preserving software source code for present and future generations.
On November 24, 2026 the archive's public counters showed 31,512,603,597 unique source files, 6,446,026,817 commits and 463,285,723 project origins.
